title: Breathings and Accents
description: Breathings, the three accents, and the rules that fix where an accent may stand.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Every word that begins with a vowel or diphthong carries a breathing: rough (῾, an h sound) or smooth (᾿, no sound). Words also carry one accent: acute (´), grave (`) or circumflex (῀). The accent can stand only on one of the last three syllables, and the length of the last syllable limits where it may go.

blocks.caption: Breathings
rows: On a diphthong the breathing stands over the second vowel: υἱός, οἶκος. ρ at the start of a word always has the rough breathing (ῥῆμα). The iota subscript, a small ι under α, η or ω (ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ), is a silent iota; it must be written, and the course always checks it.

blocks.caption: Accents
blocks.html: The last three syllables are the ultima, the penult and the antepenult. The acute may stand on any of them; the circumflex only on a long vowel or diphthong in the ultima or penult; the grave only on the ultima. If the ultima is long, the acute cannot stand on the antepenult (ἄνθρωπος but ἀνθρώπου) and a long penult takes an acute, not a circumflex (δῶρον but δώρου). An acute on the ultima becomes grave when another word follows without punctuation: ἀδελφός, but ἀδελφὸς βλέπει.

blocks.caption: How the course checks accents
blocks.html: On the lower typing rungs the course checks letters, breathings and the iota subscript. On the top rung it checks the accents too; a grave typed as an acute is accepted, and so is either form of an accent that a following enclitic changes.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: αι and οι count as short at the end of a word for accent purposes (ἄνθρωποι), except in the optative. The breathing of a capital stands before it: Ἰησοῦς.
